# Data quality: why this study re-derives runs scored

The question turns on the exact score after every play, so the run count per play has to be right. The mart's `play.runs_on_play` is not, often enough to matter.

## Final scores that match the game logs

| Runs per play from | Games matching the official final | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `play.runs_on_play` (stored) | 174,995 of 201,870 | 86.7% |
| re-derived from the event string | 199,506 of 201,870 | 98.8% |

The derived count is the one this study uses. See `RUNS` in `queries.ts` for the rule.

## Two bugs in the stored column

**Phantom runs on force outs.** A run is credited on plays like `64(1)/FO` and `5(2)/FO` that have no advance section at all — no runner is written as reaching home, so no run scored. **19,646** plays across **18,582** games.

**Dropped runs on multi-run plays.** Fewer runs credited than there are advances to home in the event, typically when a second run is marked `(UR)`: `S9/L9M.3-H;2-H(UR);1-3` scores two, the mart records one. **6,092** plays across **5,404** games.

Both change the answer to this question. Two games — Jun 8, 1989 (PIT @ PHI) and Aug 21, 1990 (PHI @ LAN) — are false positives created by a phantom run, and they drop out once runs are derived. One game — Sep 4, 2002 (KCA @ OAK) — is a false negative: a dropped run left the ninth-inning tie showing as 11–10, hiding a genuine blown 11-run lead.

## What this study cannot see

**462** of the **1,120** candidate games (both teams 11+ runs) have a game log but no play-by-play, so their trajectory is unknowable here — 1871-05-05 to 1955-04-16, overwhelmingly the pre-1900 game.
